deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. The previous folio (38r) works with the n-th Fourier mode, cos n(θ−ψ), of a problem on the unit disc. The key operator there is the double Abel-type kernel K_n(x,y) = ∫_{max(x,y)}^1 z^{-2n+2}(z^2−x^2)^{-1/2}(z^2−y^2)^{-1/2} dz. A family of functions g_n is used together with the moment formula
∫_0^1 ξ^{n−1}(1−ξ^2)^{-1/2} g_n(ξ/r) dξ = r^n · ½ Π(−½)^3 Π(n−1)/Π(n−½) for r<1,
and the reflection rule r g_n(r) = g_n(1/r). Notation is Gauss's Π(s)=Γ(s+1), so Π(−½)=√π. On this folio Riemann (a) checks that the g_n-transform inverts the K_n-transform, (b) treats a related 'integrated' form of the kernel, and (c) sums the Fourier modes into a closed-form kernel.

BLOCK 1 (inversion check). Define 𝔉_1(y) = ∫_0^1 y^{n−1} g_n(t/y) t^n dp_t, a Stieltjes integral against a function p. Then
πγ(p_x − p_1) = ∫_0^1 𝔉_1(y) d_y ∫_x^1 z^{−2n+2}(z^2−x^2)^{−1/2}(z^2−y^2)^{−1/2} dz.
- Insert 𝔉_1 and exchange the order of integration, with t outermost. One trial line is struck out.
- Rewrite the y-part as t^{2n} ∂/∂t of ∫_x^1 z^{−2n+2}(z^2−x^2)^{−1/2} dz ∫_0^z y^{n−2}(z^2−y^2)^{−1/2} t^{−n+1} g_n(t/y) dy.
- Scale y = zρ and z = x/γ, giving ∫_0^1 γ^{n−1}(1−γ^2)^{−1/2} x^{−n} dγ ∫_0^1 ρ^{n−2}(1−ρ^2)^{−1/2} t^{−n+1} g_n(...) dρ.
- Evaluate the inner ρ-integral with the moment formula of 38r (the reflection rule is used where the argument exceeds 1).
- Split t>x from t<x. For t>x the result is t^{2n} ∂_t[ t^{−2n+1} ∫_0^1 ρ^{2n−2}(1−ρ^2)^{−1/2} dρ ] · ½Π(−½)^3 Π(n−1)/Π(n−½). The t<x part has an x^{−2n+1} prefactor and an incomplete integral; its upper limit is illegible.
- Conclusion: the whole equals −(Π(−½))^4 ∫_x^1 dp = −π^2 (p_1 − p_x).
So the g_n-transform inverts the K_n-transform up to the constant π^2, which fixes γ.

BLOCK 2 (integrated kernel). The left side is n·[?](u_1 − p_1/2n) − (p_1/2n) x^{2n}. It is set equal to
∫_0^1 𝔉_1(y) d ∫_1^x r^{2n−1} dr ∫ z^{−2n+2}(z^2−r^2)^{−1/2}(z^2−y^2)^{−1/2} dz.
- Substitute z → rz. The powers of r collapse to r^1, giving ∫_x^1 r dr ∫_1^{1/r} z^{−2n+2}(z^2−1)^{−1/2}(r^2z^2−y^2)^{−1/2} dz. The ordering 1/x > 1/r > z > 1 is noted on the page.
- Swap the order (for fixed z, r runs from x to 1/z). Use ∫ r (r^2z^2−y^2)^{−1/2} dr = z^{−2}√(r^2z^2−y^2). This gives
−∫_0^1 𝔉_1(y) d ∫_1^{1/x} z^{−2n}(z^2−1)^{−1/2}(√(1−y^2) − √(z^2x^2−y^2)) dz.
- Rescale z → z/x. The √(z^2−y^2) term becomes x^{2n} ∫_y^1 z^{−2n}(z^2−x^2)^{−1/2}(z^2−y^2)^{1/2} dz.
- For the √(1−y^2) term (my reading): write −∫_x^1 = ∫_1^∞ − ∫_x^∞. Since ∫_x^∞ z^{−2n}(z^2−x^2)^{−1/2} dz = c_n x^{−2n}, that piece is an x-independent constant after multiplying by x^{2n}, so it can be absorbed into the constant terms on the left. What remains is x^{2n} ∫_1^∞ z^{−2n}(z^2−x^2)^{−1/2}(1−y^2)^{1/2} dz, as written.

BLOCK 3 (mode summation, closed-form kernel). The full solution is
π^3 u(x,ψ) = Σ_{n=−∞}^{∞} ∫_0^1 dy ∫_{−π}^{π} v(y,θ) cos n(θ−ψ) dθ ∫ (y^n x^n / z^{2n})(z^2−x^2)^{−1/2}(z^2−y^2)^{−1/2} dz + (an analogous term with (1−y^2)^{1/2} and z from 1 to ∞).
- Substitute z^2 = xy·r. The Fourier sum becomes Σ r^{−|n|} cos nφ = (r^2−1)/(r^2 − 2r cos φ + 1), a Poisson kernel.
- The measure becomes dz/√((z^2−x^2)(z^2−y^2)) = dr / (2√(xy) √((r−x/y)(r−y/x) r)).
- Result: π^3 u(x,ψ) = ∫_0^1 dy ∫_{−π}^{π} dθ v(y,θ) Ω, with
Ω = (1/(2√(xy))) ∫_{x/y}^{1/(xy)} dr/√((r−x/y)(r−y/x) r) · (r^2−1)/(r^2−2cos(θ−ψ) r+1)
+ (1/2)(1−y^2)^{−1/2} ∫_{1/(xy)}^{∞} (…)(r^2−1)/(r^2−2cos(θ−ψ)r+1) dr.
- The last line restates the first term in the cleaned form 1/(2√(yx)) ∫ dr/√((r−x/y)(r−y/x)r) · (r^2−1)/(r^2−2cos(θ−ψ)r+1).

What the page serves (my inference): an explicit closed-form solving kernel for a mixed (disc-type) potential problem on the unit disc in polar coordinates (y,θ). It is built by Abel-type transforms mode by mode, then summed with the Poisson kernel. This is the structure of the later Copson-type solution of the electrified-disc / disc Dirichlet problem.
errors: Block 1, t>x part: with ∫_0^1 ρ^{2n−2}(1−ρ^2)^{−1/2}dρ = ½B(n−½,½) and the factor ½Π(−½)^3Π(n−1)/Π(n−½), the constant is π^2/(4(n−½)). Then t^{2n}∂_t t^{−2n+1} = (1−2n), so this part gives −(π^2/2)∫_x^1 dp, not −π^2∫_x^1 dp. Either the t<x part (partly illegible) supplies the other half, or there is a factor-2 slip. This cannot be settled from the image.
Block 3: the lower limit of the r-integral is written as x/y. Since z must exceed both x and y, it should be max(x/y, y/x); as written this is valid only for y<x (or the case split is implicit).

Block 2: in the step yielding (√(1−y^2) − √(z^2x^2−y^2)), the constraint zx>y is silently ignored. Also, the passage from −∫_x^1 to ∫_1^∞ for the √(1−y^2) term relies on absorbing a constant c_n·x^{−2n}·x^{2n} into the left side. This is not written out.
The transcription's limits ∫_1^x in Block 3 should most likely read from max(x,y) to 1; the order and limits on the page are loose.

results.what: Inversion of a double Abel-type kernel ∫ z^{2−2n}(z^2−x^2)^{−1/2}(z^2−y^2)^{−1/2}dz by an integral transform with kernel functions g_n, verified via Beta-integral moments
results.modern_name: Abel/Erdélyi–Kober fractional-integral factorization of the disc kernel (Copson's method for mixed boundary value problems)
results.usually_credited_to: E. T. Copson (1947), with antecedents in Beltrami (1881) and Kobayashi (1931)

results.what: Reduction of an iterated r-z integral by the scaling z→rz and an order swap to an elementary square-root expression
Summation of the Fourier modes with the Poisson kernel after substituting z^2 = xy·r, giving a closed-form kernel Ω(x,ψ;y,θ) for a disc problem
results.modern_name: Closed-form Green-type kernel for the circular-disc mixed boundary value problem (non-axisymmetric)
results.usually_credited_to: Copson (1947); related closed forms by Hobson (1900)

deep.surprise_reason: If the inferred interpretation is right, Riemann had a working version of the Abel-transform (Copson-type) solution of a non-axisymmetric disc problem. This includes mode-by-mode inversion and a Poisson-summed closed kernel, decades before Copson (1947). The interpretation is inferred from structure, the page is fragmentary with a possible factor-2 slip, and similar methods appear in the 19th century (Beltrami, Hobson). So the score is moderate rather than high.
